meters.label: Classes hit by one base change

frames.narration: A base Unit class with a move method, and subclasses that override it. For one kind of movement this is simple and fine.

Designers want swimmers, flyers and animals that do several things, plus melee and ranged attackers. Each combination needs a class, and a class can inherit only one parent, so the other behaviours are copied in.
With 3 movements and 2 attacks there are 14 unit classes and 24 copies of ability code. A sixth ability would mean 126 classes.

The base class is also fragile. A subclass that counts adds by overriding add and addAll was right only because the old addAll called add. Rewrite the base and the counts change with no edit to the subclass.
Composition starts by splitting the axes: one small class for each ability, behind one interface for movement and one for attack. The Unit holds parts and delegates to them.
A duck is a Unit built with walk, swim and fly. A frog is built with walk and swim. No new class is needed for a new combination, and the 3 behaviour classes are written once.
A new ability, say dive, is one new class. The base change problem shrinks too: parts only meet the Unit through a small interface, so one change reaches one class.

Composition costs wiring: every unit type is assembled somewhere, and forwarding calls is boilerplate. Keep a little inheritance for true is-a cases and framework hooks. The slogan is a default, not a ban.
